newsitem.title: FRANCE: ONIC floats rule change on EU grain export tax.
newsitem.headline: ONIC floats rule change on EU grain export tax.

text.p: A French grain industry group set up by the ONIC cereals office has proposed a change in European Union rules for grain export taxes that it says would make it easier to export when European prices nearly match world levels.

ONIC director general Alain Moulinier said on Wednesday the proposal would allow the European Commission to grant exports with both taxes and subsidies at the same weekly export tender -- something disallowed under current EU rules.
Moulinier told a news conference the idea had emerged from a newly created "exporters' commission" of grain trading firms and advisers set up to make proposals to on fine-tuning regulations.
It was designed purely to smooth the flow of exports when the difference between world and European prices was so close as to make "no fundemental difference" between taxes and subsidies.
He drew a distinction between this kind of situation, at the Thursday tenders, and heavier taxes sometimes imposed through a parallel daily system to halt exports for policy reasons.
The EU reinstated such a tax on Wednesday after a week's delay caused by a French EU Commissioner's opposition.
The EU's current framework allows traders to include either refunds or taxes in their tender bids whenever an enabling tax regulation is in force.
But the Commission does not allow itself to accept both taxes and subsidies at the same tender for one type of grain.

Moulinier argued this could frustrate export trade in some circumstances by allowing one operator to block a competitor's attempt to secure refunds by putting in an affordable offer to pay a tax that the Commission would have to accept first.
Faced with just such a situation in the past year, the Commission has rejected all bids and offers, analysts said.
It was not clear whether how Brussels would greet the plan.

One operator said it might expose Brussels to complaints from those who were forking out taxes while others were still getting subsidy. It also ran counter to the Commission's declared aim of selling always at the lowest budgetary cost.
Moulinier said the proposed freedom to issue both kinds of export licence would however be restricted to a narrow "grey zone," in which world and EU prices were very close.
Issues of principle between subsidy and tax would then no longer exist and the market could do business more effectively.
"This system is only acceptable in a band close to zero," he said, referring to the price gap between EU and world prices.
He said it would prevent the EU having to chop and change between different kinds of regulation as markets fluctuated either side of the zero price differential.
Moulinier said ONIC had yet to discuss the idea with the European Commission.
